transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: Amsterdam has become the first major European city to pass strict "right to repair" legislation that requires manufacturers of electronics and household appliances to make spare parts available to consumers at reasonable prices for at least five years after a product is released. The new law, which goes into effect next January, also requires manufacturers to design products that are easier to take apart and repair, rather than being glued or welded shut as many modern devices are. City officials say the legislation is aimed at reducing electronic waste, which makes up over 50 million tons globally each year and is one of the fastest growing waste streams in the world. Under the new rules, companies that fail to comply will face fines of up to 10 percent of their annual revenue in the Netherlands. The law applies to smartphones, laptops, washing machines, refrigerators, vacuum cleaners, and even small household appliances like coffee makers. Repair shops have praised the new law, saying that currently it is often more expensive to fix a broken device than to buy a new one, a practice they call "planned obsolescence." Several other European cities are now considering similar legislation, and the European Union is currently drafting a continent-wide right to repair directive expected to be finalized next year.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: A small town in central Japan has found a thoughtful way to include people with autism, sensory processing disorders, and PTSD in summer festival traditions: silent fireworks. Instead of the loud explosions that characterize typical fireworks displays, the town of Tsu uses specially designed fireworks that produce bright colors and beautiful visual effects but create almost no sound. The idea was first proposed by a local mother whose autistic son would become terrified and have panic attacks during traditional fireworks festivals. Town officials worked with fireworks manufacturers for two years to develop the special low-noise pyrotechnics. The first silent fireworks display was held last summer and was a huge success, attracting not just people with sensory sensitivities but also elderly residents, families with sleeping babies, and even pet owners whose dogs had previously been terrified of the loud noises. This year, the town expanded the event to three separate displays and added special viewing areas with wheelchair access and quiet spaces for anyone who needed to take a break. Several other towns across Japan have already contacted Tsu officials about hosting their own silent fireworks events next year.
Questions 4 and 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
4. What is special about the fireworks in Tsu?
5. Who first proposed the idea of silent fireworks?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: A group of family farmers in the Brazilian Amazon are working to restore sections of rainforest by planting native tree species on their land. The project, which started five years ago with just 12 families, has now grown to include over 300 farming households and has planted more than 2 million trees. Unlike many environmental projects that require farmers to completely stop using their land, this initiative teaches farmers to plant corridors of native trees between their fields and pastures. These forest corridors connect remaining patches of rainforest, allowing birds and animals to move safely between areas and helping to restore biodiversity. Farmers have also found that the trees improve soil quality, provide shade for their cattle during dry seasons, and produce extra income from fruits, nuts, and sustainable timber. Researchers studying the project have found that water quality in local streams has improved significantly, and several species of birds that had not been seen in the area for decades have returned. The project has been so successful that the Brazilian government is now planning to expand the model to other regions of the Amazon.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.

7. How many trees have been planted so far?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Chloe): Jake, I think we need to finalize our plans for the camping trip this weekend! It's already Wednesday, and we haven't even decided where we're going yet.

Man (Jake): Relax, Chloe, I've been looking at campgrounds. There's Pine Ridge State Park about two hours away, or Maple Lake which is about an hour and a half closer. Pine Ridge has better hiking trails, but Maple Lake has canoe rentals and swimming areas.

Woman: Hmm, I definitely want to go swimming since it's going to be 85 degrees all weekend. But good hiking would be nice too. Wait, does Maple Lake have showers? Because I remember last time we went camping at that place without showers, I felt disgusting by Sunday morning.

Man: Yeah, Maple Lake has hot showers and flush toilets, which is definitely a plus. Pine Ridge only has pit toilets and no showers. Also, I checked the availability, and Maple Lake still has campsites available for this weekend, but Pine Ridge is completely booked.
Woman: Perfect, Maple Lake it is then! Now, what about food? Last time we went camping, everyone just brought chips and candy, and I felt sick the whole time. Can we plan actual meals this time?
Man: Agreed. I can bring my portable grill and some burgers and hot dogs. Could you bring breakfast stuff? Pancake mix, eggs, orange juice?
Woman: Sure, I can bring that, plus some vegetables and fruit. We should make sure we have plenty of water too - I'll bring a couple large jugs. What about tents and sleeping bags? Do we have enough?

Man: My tent sleeps four, and Mike said he can bring his three-person tent. That's enough for the five of us. I have extra sleeping bags too, I think. Wait, actually, we need to ask Lisa if she has her own, because last time she forgot hers and had to share with Sarah.
Woman: I'll text Lisa about that. What time do you want to leave on Friday? We should try to get there before dark so we can set up camp easily.

Man: I get out of my statistics class at 2 PM, so if everyone can be at my apartment by 3, we can leave by 3:30. That would get us there around 5, before the sun sets at 6:30. We should also remember to bring flashlights and extra batteries, just in case.
Woman: Good call. Oh, and don't forget the bug spray! The mosquitoes are terrible this time of year, especially near the lake.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: Yawning is something we all do, often multiple times a day, but scientists have long been puzzled about exactly why we yawn and why yawns seem to be contagious. For many years, the common belief was that yawning was the body's way of bringing more oxygen into the bloodstream when we were tired or bored. However, research conducted over the past 15 years has largely disproven this theory, finding that breathing air with higher levels of oxygen does not reduce yawning. The current leading theory, supported by multiple brain imaging studies, is that yawning helps cool the brain. When you yawn, the deep inhalation of air and the stretching of the jaw increases blood flow to the brain, and the incoming air cools that blood, helping to maintain optimal brain temperature. This would explain why people yawn more when they are tired, as brain temperature rises when we are fatigued. As for why yawns are contagious? Research suggests this is related to human empathy. Studies have consistently found that people who score higher on empathy tests are more likely to catch yawns from others, while people with conditions that reduce empathy, like severe autism, are less likely to experience contagious yawning. Even reading about yawning or seeing someone yawn on video is enough to trigger the response in most people - and if you've yawned while listening to this, you're certainly not alone.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: In cities where housing costs have skyrocketed over the past two decades, micro-apartments have become an increasingly popular housing option. These tiny living spaces, typically between 150 and 300 square feet, are designed to maximize every inch of space with built-in furniture, lofted beds, fold-down tables, and clever storage solutions. Cities like Tokyo, Hong Kong, New York, and London have seen a boom in micro-apartment construction, as developers try to create more affordable housing in expensive urban centers. Proponents argue that micro-apartments provide an affordable option for young professionals, students, and single people who want to live in desirable city locations but cannot afford traditional apartments. They point out that many people living alone in large apartments rarely use most of their living space, and that well-designed micro-apartments can feel larger than their square footage suggests. Critics, however, argue that micro-apartments are too small for comfortable long-term living, and that they represent a decline in housing standards. Some cities have even passed laws setting minimum apartment sizes to prevent developers from building extremely tiny units. Despite the controversy, micro-apartments continue to grow in popularity, with many buildings offering shared amenities like communal kitchens, rooftop gardens, gyms, and co-working spaces to make up for the small private living areas.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Board games have been a popular form of entertainment for thousands of years, with the earliest known board game dating back over 5,000 years to ancient Egypt. That game, called Senet, was played on a 30-square board and was so popular that even Egyptian pharaohs were buried with Senet boards to enjoy in the afterlife. Many other ancient cultures developed their own board games as well: the ancient Greeks played a game called Petteia, the Chinese invented Go over 2,500 years ago, and the Indian game of Chaturanga is the ancestor of all modern chess. Board games remained popular through the Middle Ages and into the 19th century, when companies began mass-producing games like Snakes and Ladders and Ludo. However, the 20th century brought a massive boom in board game popularity, especially in the United States during the Great Depression. Monopoly, introduced in 1935, became a massive hit because it allowed people to fantasize about wealth and property ownership at a time when many had very little money. The 1990s and 2000s saw the rise of modern "Eurogames" from Germany, like Settlers of Catan, which emphasized strategy and social interaction over simple luck. Today, board games are more popular than ever, with thousands of new games released each year covering every possible theme, from farming to space exploration to cooperative zombie survival.
